title: Cap. VI: Maresius args IV–V — Rom. 5:12 peccavimus; Levi in Abraham's loins
pass_a_gloss: Fourth, Maresius asks who would deny that what we have sinned is rightly imputed to us, and says the Apostle teaches that sin is ours too because all sinned in Adam (Romans 5:12). Placeus grants that what we have sinned is justly imputed — but our sinning is prior, at least by nature's order, to that imputation. Cut away imputation in thought, and show if you can that we committed the first man's first actual sin. Those who hold antecedent imputation say that sin is ours only by imputation — so it is ours because it is imputed, not imputed because it is ours. As for the Apostle, peccavimus does not signify Adam's first actual sin, and Placeus reads eo quod rather than in quo; even in quo yields at most consequent or mediate imputation, to be shown later. Fifth, Maresius argues from Levi tithed in Abraham's loins (Hebrews 7:9) to our all having sinned in Adam's loins as branches in a root, mass in firstfruits, members in a head (Romans 11:16; 1 Corinthians 15:22). Placeus asks: if someone argued the same from Seth's or Enosh's or any pre-flood patriarch's loins, would Maresius grant the consequence? There is none — nothing picks Adam's first actual sin over later ones, Adam over Seth or Noah, or antecedent over consequent. Freely granting we sinned in Adam's loins does not yield antecedent imputation before hereditary corruption; rather the contrary. We sinned in Adam because we were in him as branches in a root — and branches properly have nothing of the root imputed, but draw nature and sap as the root is. So we drew corrupt nature from corrupt Adam. The mass was not properly in the firstfruits, nor other members in the head; these comparisons are foreign and induce no imputation, least of all immediate or antecedent.
pass_b_english: IV. To the former the distinguished Maresius joins certain other arguments. And who indeed, he says, would deny that what we have sinned is deservedly and rightly imputed to us? But that that sin is ours also, the Apostle clearly teaches, who asserts that all have sinned in Adam. Romans 5:12. Wholly, what we have sinned is deservedly imputed to us. But that sinning of ours is prior, at least by order of nature, to the imputation itself. Therefore cut away imputation by thought, and show us, if you can, that we have sinned the very first actual sin of the first man. Those who hold antecedent imputation say that that sin is not ours except by imputation. If it is not ours except by imputation, it is ours because it is imputed to us, not on the contrary imputed to us because it is ours. As to what touches the Apostle's place, neither by the word we have sinned is the first actual sin of Adam signified, nor does the Apostle seem to us to say in whom but rather in that, nor if you turn it in whom can any imputation therefore be elicited, unless perhaps consequent or mediate, as in its place, God granting, I am going to demonstrate.

V. He adds, For if in Abraham's loins Levi was tithed, Hebrews 7:9, how much more shall we all be judged to have sinned in Adam's loins, inasmuch as we were in him as branches in a root, a mass in firstfruits, members in a head, Romans 11:16, 1 Corinthians 15:22. If anyone should argue similarly: If in Abraham's loins Levi was tithed, how much more in the loins of Seth, or of Enosh, or of some other of the Patriarchs who lived before the flood, have we all sinned? Would the learned man prove the consequence? Or what could he answer that could not be likewise answered to him? There is therefore no consequence. For by what art will the imputation of the first actual sin be elicited from there rather than of following sins, and of Adam's rather than of Seth's or Noah's, and antecedent rather than consequent? But, that I may act liberally, I confess that we have sinned in Adam's loins: does it therefore follow that his first actual sin is imputed to us by an imputation which precedes hereditary corruption? The contrary rather follows. For we have sinned in Adam, because we were in him. But we were in him as branches in a root. And branches are so in a root that nothing of the root is properly imputed to the branches, but the branches draw from the root their nature and vital sap, such as is in the root, good or bad. So we have drawn a corrupt nature from corrupt Adam. For the rest, neither was the mass properly in the firstfruits, but the firstfruits in the mass, nor other members in the head. And so these comparisons seem foreign from what we are doing, and induce no imputation, much less an immediate or antecedent one.
source_text:
IV. Superioribus alia quaedam Cl. Maresius adiungit argumenta. Ecquis vero, inquit, neget quod nos peccavimus, nobis merito iureque imputari? Iam autem nostrum esse quoque illud peccatum, clare docet Apostolus, qui omnes in Adamo peccasse asserit. Rom. 5. 12. Omnino quod nos peccavimus, nobis merito imputatur. Sed illud peccare nostrum prius est, saltem ordine naturae, ipsa illius imputatione. Praescinde ergo cogitatione imputationem, nosque si potes, demonstra peccasse ipsum primum actuale peccatum primi hominis. Qui antecedentem imputationem tenent, aiunt peccatum illud nostrum non esse nisi per imputationem. Si nostrum non est nisi imputatione, nostrum est quia nobis imputatur, non contra nobis imputatur quia nostrum est. Ad locum Apostoli quod attinet, nec verbo peccavimus primum actuale Adae peccatum significatur, nec Apostolus nobis videtur dicere in quo sed eo quod potius, nec si vertas in quo propterea elici ulla poterit imputatio, nisi forte consequens seu mediata, ut suo loco, Deo dante, demonstraturus sum.

V. Addit, Si enim in Abrahae lumbis decimatus est Levi, Heb. vii. 9. quanto magis in lumbis Adami nos omnes peccasse censebimur, utpote qui in illo essemus ut rami in radice, massa in primitiis, membra in capite, Rom. xi. 16. 1. Cor. xv. 22. Si quis similiter argumentaretur: Si in Abrahae lumbis decimatus est Levi, quanto magis in lumbis Sethi, vel Enoschi, vel alterius alicuius Patriarcharum qui ante diluvium vixerunt, nos omnes peccavimus? Probaretne consequentiam vir doctus? aut quid posset respondere, quod ei reponi similiter non possit? Nulla igitur est consequentia. Qua enim arte inde elicietur imputatio primi peccati actualis potius quam sequentium, et Adami potius quam Sethi aut Noachi, et antecedens potius quam consequens? Sed, ut liberaliter agam, fateor nos in lumbis Adami peccasse: num inde sequitur, nobis eius primum actuale peccatum imputari imputatione quae corruptionem haereditariam antecedat? sequitur contrarium potius. Peccavimus enim in Adamo, quia in eo fuimus. Fuimus autem in eo ut rami in radice. Ita autem sunt rami in radice, ut nihil radicis ramis imputetur proprie, sed trahant rami a radice naturam suam et succum vitalem, qualis est in radice, bonum vel malum. Sic nos ab Adamo corrupto naturam corruptam traximus. Ceterum nec massa in primitiis proprie fuit, sed in massa primitiae, nec alia membra in capite. Itaque hae comparationes ab eo quod agimus alienae videntur, nec ullam imputationem inducunt, nedum immediatam aut antecedentem.
